# Exercise 9.1 — Importance, and a column of pure noise {#sec-importance}


## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Fit a random forest and read two different importance rankings off it.
- State, for each measure, what it is a measure of and which question it
  answers.
- Use a pure-noise control to decide how much of a ranking to believe.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-random-forest left you with a forest that predicts better than the
logistic regression of @sec-logistic-regression and cannot be read. The obvious
next move is to ask the forest which variables it used. Every library will
answer that question. The problem is that they answer different questions, give
different rankings, and none of them will tell you so. We settle it the way you
would settle any measurement question: by measuring something whose true value
we already know.

## The model we will spend the day explaining

We add one predictor that cannot possibly matter — a column of random numbers,
drawn independently of everything else, named `noise`. It is not a trick on the
model. It is a control on the *importance measures*: whatever any of them says
about `noise`, we know the right answer is nothing.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(parsnip); library(rsample)
library(yardstick); library(vip); library(ggplot2)

set.seed(123)
dia <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")),
         noise    = round(rnorm(n()), 2))

split <- initial_split(dia, prop = 0.7, strata = diabetes)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

rf_fit <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

preds <- predict(rf_fit, test, type = "prob") |> bind_cols(test)
roc_auc(preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

dia = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
y = (dia["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
X = dia.drop(columns=["diabetes"]).copy()
X["noise"] = np.random.default_rng(42).normal(size=len(X)).round(2)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=123, stratify=y)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(X_train, y_train)
auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
round(auc, 3)
```
:::

Both forests score a test AUC in the high 0.7s. Note the `event_level =
"second"` in the R call: the factor levels are `neg`, `pos`, and **yardstick
treats the first level as the event**, so without that argument you would be
scoring the model's ability to detect *absence* of diabetes.

## Measure 1 — impurity importance

Every split in every tree reduces Gini impurity by some amount. Impurity
importance adds those reductions up, per variable, over the whole forest. It is
free: the forest already computed it while fitting. It is also entirely
internal — it is a summary of what happened inside the training rows, and no
test data enters it anywhere.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
imp <- vi(rf_fit)
imp
vip(rf_fit, num_features = 9) + labs(title = "Impurity importance")
```

## Python

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
imp = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values()
print(imp.round(3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
imp.plot(kind="barh", ax=ax, color="steelblue")
ax.set_xlabel("mean decrease in impurity")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Stuck?
The check wants the importances themselves, not the model. In R that is the
object `vi()` returned; in Python it is the `Series` you built from
`feature_importances_`. The check finds `noise` by name.
:::

The check prints `[fix]`. **That is not a mistake in your code.** It is the
check doing its job on a measure that has just handed a third of its top score
to a column of random numbers.

## Task 2 — Ask a different question

Permutation importance asks something else entirely: *if I destroy this
variable, how much worse does the model get?* Shuffle one column of the **test**
set, re-score, record the drop in AUC, put the column back, repeat. Nothing is
refitted; the model is held fixed and the data is damaged.

Fill in the two blanks: which rows to permute, and which metric to score.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
pred_pos <- function(object, newdata) predict(object, newdata, type = "prob")$.pred_pos

set.seed(123)
perm <- vi(rf_fit, method = "permute",
           train = ______, target = "diabetes",
           metric = ______, event_level = "second",
           pred_wrapper = pred_pos, nsim = 20,
           smaller_is_better = FALSE)
perm
check_noise_control(perm)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
pred_pos <- function(object, newdata) predict(object, newdata, type = "prob")$.pred_pos

set.seed(123)
perm <- vi(rf_fit, method = "permute",
           train = test, target = "diabetes",
           metric = "roc_auc", event_level = "second",
           pred_wrapper = pred_pos, nsim = 20,
           smaller_is_better = FALSE)
perm
check_noise_control(perm)
```
:::
:::

## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
result = permutation_importance(rf, X_test, y_test, n_repeats=20,
                                random_state=123, scoring="roc_auc")
perm = pd.Series(result.importances_mean, index=X.columns).sort_values()
print(perm.round(4))
check_noise_control(perm)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
Permutation importance needs rows the model has not been fitted on, and a
metric to measure the damage with. You have both already: the held-out set, and
the AUC you reported above. In Python the metric is a string scikit-learn
recognises; in R it is a yardstick metric name.
:::

This time the check passes. Under permutation the control is worth a few per
cent of glucose at most, which is what zero looks like once sampling noise is
added to it. Report which variables changed rank between the two measures.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Below the top two, the ordering is not real
In both languages glucose dominates and age is a distant second. Everything
below that is a cluster of near-zero values whose spread across repeats is as
large as the values themselves — `noise` finishes inside that cluster, in R
slightly above zero and in Python slightly below it. Do not report a rank order
within a cluster like that. Report the cluster.
:::

## The result that should bother you

Impurity importance put `noise` fifth of nine, ahead of blood pressure,
insulin and triceps skinfold — three measurements a diabetes clinic actually
takes. Reason it through in three steps.

1. The forest is allowed to split on `noise`, and with `mtry = 3` it is offered
   the chance about a third of the time. A continuous variable with 768
   distinct-ish values offers a great many candidate split points, so by chance
   some of them separate the training rows well.
2. Each of those lucky splits reduces training impurity, and impurity
   importance counts every one of them. Nothing in the measure asks whether the
   reduction survives on rows the forest has not seen.
3. So impurity importance is a faithful description of *how the forest was
   built*. It is not evidence about which variables carry signal. Those are
   different claims, and only the second one is what anybody wants.

This is not an obscure edge case. It is the default output of
`feature_importances_` and of `vip()`, it appears in papers, and the control
that exposes it costs one line.

## Task 3 — Is the noise column doing any harm?

If impurity importance is right that `noise` matters, dropping it should hurt.
Refit the forest without it and compare test AUC.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rf_clean <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = ______)

predict(rf_clean, test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
rf_clean <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 3, min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 123) |>
  set_mode("classification") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ ., data = select(train, -noise))

predict(rf_clean, test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(test) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rf_clean = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(
    X_train.drop(columns=______), y_train)
auc_clean = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_clean.predict_proba(
    X_test.drop(columns=______))[:, 1])
print(round(auc_clean, 3), "versus", round(auc, 3), "with the noise column")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rf_clean = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=123).fit(
    X_train.drop(columns=["noise"]), y_train)
auc_clean = roc_auc_score(y_test, rf_clean.predict_proba(
    X_test.drop(columns=["noise"]))[:, 1])
print(round(auc_clean, 3), "versus", round(auc, 3), "with the noise column")
```
:::
:::
:::

The AUC moves by about one point in the second decimal — in Python it goes up a
little, in R down a little. That is the same size as the spread you get from
refitting the forest with ten different seeds and changing nothing else, so it
is not a difference at all. A variable that one importance measure ranked
fifth of nine is worth nothing to the prediction.

## Reflection

1. Impurity importance and permutation importance disagreed. Write the sentence
   you would say to a clinical collaborator who asks which one is correct —
   without using the word "wrong".
2. Permutation importance is computed on held-out rows here. What would change
   if you computed it on the training rows instead, and which of the two would
   you report in a paper?
3. You now have a control for *importance*. What would the equivalent control
   be for a claim that the model is well calibrated?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) Something like: "they measure different things — one counts how
often the forest used a variable while it was being built, the other measures
how much the predictions degrade without it. Only the second is about
prediction." The useful follow-up is to ask which one the collaborator thought
they were being shown. (2) On training rows the drop is dominated by
memorisation, so every variable the forest leaned on looks important, including
the control; the held-out version is the one to report, and it is also the one
with a defensible interpretation — generalisation loss. (3) A control for
calibration is a model whose probabilities are deliberately distorted, for
example by pushing every prediction towards 0.5, and then checking that your
calibration diagnostic actually notices.

**Expected values** (regenerating the data moves the last digit).
Test AUC 0.75–0.80 in both languages. Impurity: glucose first at roughly four
times the control; `noise` fifth of nine at 30–37% of glucose. Permutation on
the test set: glucose 0.14–0.17, everything else under 0.02, `noise` between
−0.01 and +0.01. Refitting without `noise` changes AUC by under 0.015 in either
direction.

**Common failures.** (1) Passing the fitted model rather than the importance
table to `check_noise_control()`. (2) In R, omitting `event_level = "second"`,
which silently reports AUC for the wrong class — the giveaway is an AUC near
0.2. (3) Reading the `[fix]` in Task 1 as a bug and trying to debug it; say
early that a check can fail honestly. (4) Treating the permutation ranking
below the top two as meaningful.

**Timing.** If you are short, set Task 3 as a demonstration rather than an
exercise — but do not skip it, because it is the only direct evidence that the
control is worthless to the prediction rather than merely low-ranked.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — Two controls, not one
Add a second control: a column of integers `1:n`, a row identifier. It carries
no information either, but it has one distinct value per patient. Where does
impurity importance put it, and what does the comparison with `noise` tell you
about which features that measure favours?
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Correlated predictors break both measures
Add a copy of `glucose` with a little jitter, so the two columns are nearly
identical. What happens to glucose's permutation importance, and why? Write
down the sentence a reader would wrongly conclude from the new ranking.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that for this forest, on these held-out rows, permuting glucose costs
about 0.14 of AUC and permuting anything else costs almost nothing; and that a
column known to be meaningless was ranked fifth of nine by the forest's own
built-in importance.

**Cannot:** anything about an individual patient. Both measures are averages
over the whole test set, and an average over 231 people cannot tell you why the
model said what it said about one of them — which is what @sec-shap is for.
